item.title: Advertising vs. Marketing: What’s the Difference?
item.dc:creator: The Caledonian-Record Business Desk
item.description:
Small-business owners often use the words advertising and marketing interchangeably.

They are related, but they are not the same thing.

Advertising is one part of marketing.

That distinction matters because a business can spend money on advertising without having a clear marketing strategy — and then conclude that “advertising doesn’t work” when the real problem is that the message, audience, offer or follow-up process was never clearly defined.

Understanding the difference can help a business spend its time and money more effectively.

Marketing Starts With the Customer

Marketing is the broader process of figuring out:

  • Who your customers are
  • What they need
  • Why they should choose you
  • What you should offer
  • How you should price it
  • Where customers are likely to find you
  • What message will resonate with them
  • How you will turn a first-time buyer into a repeat customer

Advertising comes later.

A restaurant deciding to target families with affordable weeknight meals is making a marketing decision.

So is a contractor deciding to focus on deck repairs rather than general remodeling.

So is a retailer deciding that its strongest advantage is personal service rather than the lowest possible price.

Those choices determine what the business should advertise.

Advertising Is How You Promote the Message

Advertising is paid communication designed to reach prospective customers.

That might include:

  • A newspaper ad
  • A website banner
  • A Facebook or Instagram campaign
  • Google Search ads
  • Radio
  • Direct mail
  • A sponsored newsletter
  • A billboard
  • A local event sponsorship

Advertising is essentially the distribution system for a message.

Marketing determines what the message should be.

Imagine two roofers buying identical advertisements.

One ad says:

Smith Roofing — Quality Work. Call Today.

The other says:

Leaking Roof? We Repair Asphalt and Metal Roofs Throughout Caledonia County. Free Estimates. Call 555-1234.

They may have purchased exactly the same amount of advertising.

But the second business has made better marketing decisions about the customer, service area, problem and call to action.

The advertising didn't create the difference.

The marketing did.

Marketing Includes Things You Don't Pay a Publisher or Platform For

Some of the most important marketing activities aren't traditional advertising at all.

Your Google Business Profile is marketing.

Your website is marketing.

Your customer reviews are marketing.

Your storefront signage is marketing.

How quickly you answer the phone is marketing.

The way employees treat customers is marketing.

Your estimate form, email follow-up and invoices are marketing.

Even your reputation in the community is part of your marketing.

That is why businesses should be cautious about measuring marketing only by how much they spend on ads.

A customer may see your advertisement, search your company name, read three Google reviews, visit your website and then ask a friend whether they've heard of you before finally calling.

Which thing produced the customer?

Probably all of them.

Advertising Can Generate Attention. Marketing Determines What Happens Next.

Suppose a local business runs a successful ad campaign and 500 people visit its website.

That sounds promising.

But what happens when they arrive?

If the website doesn't clearly explain the service, loads poorly on a phone or makes it difficult to contact the business, much of the advertising investment may be wasted.

The advertisement did its job.

The rest of the marketing system didn't.

The same thing can happen offline.

A restaurant can advertise a special dinner successfully and then lose future business because nobody collects customer email addresses, encourages reviews or invites those customers back.

Advertising can create an opportunity.

Marketing determines how much value the business gets from that opportunity.

Start With a Goal, Not an Ad

One of the easiest ways to waste money is to start with the question:

“Where should I advertise?”

A better first question is:

“What am I trying to accomplish?”

Those are very different conversations.

A business might want to:

  • Introduce itself to the community
  • Generate calls for a specific service
  • Sell tickets to an event
  • Increase weekday traffic
  • Reach homeowners in a particular town
  • Promote a seasonal product
  • Find new employees
  • Generate repeat business from existing customers

Each goal may require a different message and a different advertising channel.

A restaurant trying to fill tables on Tuesday nights has a much more specific marketing problem than a restaurant simply saying, “We need more advertising.”

Specific problems are easier to solve.

Know Who You Want to Reach

Good marketing also requires deciding who the customer is.

Consider a landscaping business.

“Homeowners” is a start, but it isn't very specific.

Are you trying to reach homeowners who want weekly mowing? Owners of second homes who need property maintenance? People preparing homes for sale? Customers interested in major landscape projects?

Those audiences have different needs and different values.

Once you identify the audience, advertising becomes easier to plan.

You can choose media that reaches those people and write a message designed specifically for them.

Give People a Reason to Act

Advertising often fails because it merely announces that a business exists.

Customers usually need something more useful than that.

A strong message answers several questions quickly:

What do you do?

Who is it for?

Why should I care?

Why should I choose you?

What should I do next?

That doesn't always mean offering a discount.

The reason to act might be convenience, expertise, availability, local knowledge, faster service, a specialty product or simply a reminder at the right time.

A heating contractor doesn't necessarily need to discount furnace maintenance in October. It may be enough to remind homeowners that winter is approaching and appointments are filling.

Marketing Continues After the Sale

Advertising usually focuses on getting the customer.

Marketing should also focus on keeping the customer.

For many local businesses, repeat customers are far more valuable than continually finding new ones.

That means asking questions such as:

Do we collect customer contact information?

Do we follow up?

Do we ask satisfied customers for reviews?

Do we remind customers about seasonal services?

Do we make it easy for them to refer someone else?

Do we give them a reason to return?

A business that improves those systems may increase revenue without increasing its advertising budget at all.

You Still Need Advertising

None of this means advertising is unimportant.

A great business with no visibility can remain a well-kept secret.

Advertising can introduce a company to thousands of people, create awareness, generate leads and remind existing customers that the business is still there.

But advertising works best when it supports a larger marketing plan.

Think of it this way:

Marketing decides where you want to go.

Advertising helps you get there.

The Bottom Line

Advertising and marketing are not competing ideas.

Advertising is one tool within marketing.

Marketing is the broader strategy of understanding customers, deciding what you offer, communicating why it matters and building a system that turns attention into revenue and long-term relationships.

Before buying your next ad, ask a few questions:

Who are we trying to reach?

What do we want them to do?

What problem are we solving for them?

Why should they choose us?

What happens after they respond?

Once those answers are clear, choosing the advertisement becomes much easier.

And the money you spend promoting your business has a much better chance of producing results.

This article is part of The Caledonian-Record’s Small Business Marketing series. The Caledonian-Record provides advertising and marketing services to local businesses, including some of the tools discussed in this article.

item.title: How to Market a One-Person Handyman Business
item.dc:creator: The Caledonian-Record Business Desk
item.description:
For a one-person handyman business, marketing presents an unusual problem: You need enough work to keep the calendar full, but not so much demand that you spend your evenings answering calls, writing estimates and chasing jobs you don't have time to perform.

That means the goal isn't necessarily to generate the most leads. It's to generate the right leads — from the right customers, for the kinds of jobs you actually want.

Fortunately, a solo handyman has several advantages that larger contractors don't. Customers often like dealing directly with the person who will perform the work. A good handyman can also build a substantial business through repeat customers and referrals.

The trick is making it easy for those customers to find you, understand what you do and contact you.

1. Start With Google

For most handyman businesses, one of the most valuable pieces of marketing isn't an advertisement at all. It's a complete Google Business Profile.

When someone searches for “handyman near me,” “handyman in St. Johnsbury” or “someone to repair a door,” Google often displays local businesses prominently in the results.

Make sure your profile includes your correct phone number, service area, business hours, website if you have one, and a detailed description of the work you perform.

Photos are particularly useful. You don't need professional photography. Take clear before-and-after pictures of finished projects: repaired steps, installed doors, new shelving, drywall patches, decks, trim work and other jobs that demonstrate what you do.

Most importantly, ask satisfied customers for Google reviews.

A steady collection of legitimate reviews can help prospective customers answer one of their biggest questions before they ever call: Can I trust this person in my home?

2. Be Specific About What You Do

“Handyman services” can mean almost anything. That isn't always helpful to someone searching for a particular service.

Instead, clearly list the jobs you want:

  • Door and window repairs
  • Drywall and minor carpentry
  • Deck and porch repairs
  • Painting and staining
  • Shelving and fixture installation
  • Seasonal property maintenance
  • Small home repairs
  • Rental-property maintenance

The list should reflect your actual skills, licensing requirements and the work you want more of.

Specificity also helps search engines understand your business. A page explaining your deck-repair services has a better chance of matching someone searching for deck repair than a website that simply says, “No job too small.”

3. Build a Simple Website

A one-person handyman operation doesn't need an elaborate website. It does need a credible one.

At minimum, a useful website should explain who you are, where you work, what services you provide and how to contact you. Include photographs of completed projects, testimonials or reviews, and an easy way to request an estimate.

Your service area should be obvious.

If you work in St. Johnsbury, Lyndonville, Danville and Barnet, say so. Those geographic details help both prospective customers and search engines determine whether you're the right business for the job.

And make sure the site works well on a phone. Someone standing in front of a broken door isn't necessarily going home to open a laptop.

4. Don't Underestimate Facebook

For a local handyman, Facebook can function as digital word-of-mouth.

Community groups frequently contain questions such as, “Does anyone know somebody who can repair a porch?” or “Looking for someone to install a storm door.”

Recommendations from previous customers can be extremely valuable.

Maintain a professional business page with current contact information and examples of your work. Occasionally post finished projects, useful maintenance tips or availability.

You don't need to become a social-media personality. You simply want someone who encounters your name in a recommendation to find enough evidence online to think, “This person looks legitimate.”

5. Turn Every Good Customer Into Future Business

The cheapest customer to acquire is often one who already knows you.

Keep a basic customer list containing names, email addresses, phone numbers and the type of work you've performed.

That allows you to stay in touch without constantly advertising.

A simple spring message might say you're scheduling deck repairs, exterior maintenance and other warm-weather projects. A fall message could mention weatherproofing, storm doors or other seasonal work.

This isn't about bombarding customers with marketing. It's about reminding people who already trust you that you're still available.

6. Build a Referral Network

Some of the best sources of handyman work may be other local businesses.

Realtors frequently encounter homes that need small repairs before listing or after inspection. Property managers need reliable people for maintenance. Plumbers, electricians and larger contractors may receive requests for jobs that are too small or outside their specialty.

Introduce yourself.

A handyman who answers the phone, shows up when promised and treats referred customers well can become very valuable to these professionals.

One good referral relationship can produce work for years.

7. Advertise Where Trust Already Exists

Mass advertising isn't always necessary for a one-person operation.

Look instead for audiences that overlap with your ideal customers.

That might include a local newspaper or news website, community newsletter, neighborhood publication, home-improvement guide or local event sponsorship.

The advantage of local media is context. You're not simply buying impressions from anonymous internet users. You're appearing in an environment already associated with the community you serve.

Keep the message straightforward: What do you do? Where do you do it? Why should someone trust you? How can they reach you?

8. Make It Easy to Contact You — Without Letting the Phone Run Your Life

A common problem for solo operators is that every new lead creates administrative work.

Consider using a simple online estimate-request form asking customers for their location, contact information, type of project, preferred timing and photographs of the problem.

That allows you to screen requests before spending 15 minutes on the phone discovering that the job is outside your service area or isn't something you do.

Your voicemail can help, too. Tell callers what information to leave and when they should expect to hear back.

Good marketing doesn't just generate business. It should make the business easier to operate.

9. Track Where Your Best Jobs Come From

You don't need sophisticated analytics.

Ask every new customer one question: “How did you hear about me?”

Keep track of the answers.

After six months, you may discover that Facebook generates lots of inquiries but few worthwhile jobs, while Google produces your best customers. Or perhaps a relationship with two real-estate agents produces more profitable work than all your paid advertising combined.

Spend your marketing time and money accordingly.

10. Market for the Business You Want

This may be the most important lesson.

A one-person handyman business has limited inventory: your time.

If your calendar is already packed with $150 jobs, generating twice as many $150 jobs doesn't necessarily improve the business.

Marketing can help you gradually shape the company around better work, better customers and a manageable geographic area.

If deck repairs are profitable and enjoyable, promote deck repairs. If driving 40 minutes for tiny jobs isn't worthwhile, tighten your service area. If property managers provide reliable recurring work, actively cultivate more of those relationships.

The goal isn't to become the biggest handyman company in town. It's to build a steady stream of profitable work that one person can perform well.

The Bottom Line

A one-person handyman business doesn't need a giant marketing budget or complicated strategy.

Start by making sure people can find you on Google. Clearly explain the services you provide. Show examples of good work. Collect reviews. Maintain relationships with past customers. Develop referral partners. Advertise selectively within the community.

Then measure what works.

For a solo operator, the best marketing system isn't the one that makes the phone ring constantly. It's the one that keeps the calendar comfortably full with the kinds of jobs you want.

This article is part of The Caledonian-Record’s Small Business Marketing series. The Caledonian-Record provides advertising and marketing services to local businesses, including some of the tools discussed in this article.

item.title: Your Google Business Profile May Be Your Most Important Online Storefront
item.dc:creator: The Caledonian-Record Business Desk
item.description:
For local businesses, a few minutes spent keeping Google information accurate can make the difference between winning a customer and losing one.

A potential customer needs a plumber. Or a restaurant. Or a tire shop, hair salon, electrician or hardware store.

There is a good chance the first thing that customer does is pull out a phone and search Google.

That means the first impression of your business may not be your website, your storefront or even one of your advertisements. It may be your Google Business Profile — the information that appears alongside your business in Google Search and Google Maps.

And if that information is incomplete or outdated, you may be losing customers without ever knowing it.

Google Business Profiles are free, and verified businesses can use them to manage information including their hours, phone number, website, location or service area, photos and customer reviews.

For a local business, that makes the profile worth treating as an important piece of marketing infrastructure rather than something that gets set up once and forgotten.

Start with the basics

Pull up your own business on Google as if you were a customer.

Is the phone number correct? Does the website link work? Are the hours accurate? Is the address correct? If you travel to customers instead of serving them at a storefront, is your service area properly represented?

Google recommends keeping business information complete and up to date, and says complete and accurate information can help a business appear in relevant local search results.

Hours deserve special attention.

If Google says you are open until 6 p.m. and a customer arrives at 5:15 to find the doors locked, that is more than a minor online error. You have created a disappointed customer.

Google also allows businesses to set special hours for holidays, events and other temporary changes rather than changing their regular schedule.

Put holiday-hour updates on the same checklist as changing the sign on the front door.

Tell Google exactly what you do

Your business category and service information matter, too.

Someone may know the name of your company and search specifically for it. But the larger marketing opportunity comes from people who do not know your name.

They search for things such as “electrician near me,” “best lunch nearby,” “oil change,” “roof repair” or “florist open now.”

Google says local search results are primarily influenced by relevance, distance and prominence. Providing complete and detailed information helps Google understand what a business does and match it with relevant searches.

So don't assume Google understands everything you sell simply because your business name is listed correctly.

Review your primary business category. Add appropriate services or products where available. Complete the attributes Google offers for your type of business.

The goal isn't to cram keywords into the listing. Businesses should represent themselves accurately and consistently with how they operate in the real world.

The goal is simply to give Google — and prospective customers — a clear picture of what you actually offer.

Add current photos

Photos are especially valuable for restaurants, retailers, contractors, lodging properties, auto dealers, salons and other businesses where customers want to know what they are going to encounter.

You don't necessarily need professional photography.

A clear photo of your storefront can help someone recognize the building when they arrive. A contractor can show completed projects. A restaurant can show dishes and its dining room. A retailer can show new merchandise. A service business can show its team and equipment.

And don't let the most recent photo of your business be five years old.

A handful of current, authentic images is better than a profile that looks abandoned.

Pay attention to reviews

Reviews are another highly visible part of the profile.

Businesses should periodically read new reviews and respond when appropriate — including to negative reviews. A response demonstrates that the business is paying attention to customer feedback.

You can also ask satisfied customers to review your business. Google provides businesses with a review link or QR code that can be shared with customers. What you should not do is offer discounts, free products or other incentives in exchange for reviews; Google prohibits incentivized reviews.

A thoughtful response to a complaint can sometimes be almost as valuable as a five-star review. Future customers aren't just evaluating the reviewer. They're evaluating how the business responds.

Remember that Google gets information from other places

There is one more reason to check your profile periodically: you aren't the only source Google uses.

Business information can also come from publicly available websites, third-party data and contributions from users.

In other words, incorrect information can creep in.

That makes a quick monthly check worthwhile even if nothing at your business has intentionally changed.

A 10-minute monthly habit

Once your profile is established, maintaining it doesn't have to become another major marketing project.

Set aside 10 minutes once a month and check:

  • Business hours and upcoming holiday hours
  • Phone number, address and website
  • Business category, services and attributes
  • Recent photos
  • New customer reviews
  • Any information that looks incorrect
  • Your listing from both Google Search and Google Maps

For a small business with limited time and a limited marketing budget, there aren't many opportunities simpler than this one.

Your Google Business Profile is free. Customers are already using it. And they're often looking at it at exactly the moment they're deciding where to spend their money.

Make sure what they find is accurate, current and worth choosing.

A potential customer needs a plumber. Or a restaurant. Or a tire shop, hair salon, electrician or hardware store.

There is a good chance the first thing that customer does is pull out a phone and search Google.

That means the first impression of your business may not be your website, your storefront or even one of your advertisements. It may be your Google Business Profile — the information that appears alongside your business in Google Search and Google Maps.

And if that information is incomplete or outdated, you may be losing customers without ever knowing it.

Google Business Profiles are free, and verified businesses can use them to manage information including their hours, phone number, website, location or service area, photos and customer reviews.

For a local business, that makes the profile worth treating as an important piece of marketing infrastructure rather than something that gets set up once and forgotten.

Start with the basics

Pull up your own business on Google as if you were a customer.

Is the phone number correct? Does the website link work? Are the hours accurate? Is the address correct? If you travel to customers instead of serving them at a storefront, is your service area properly represented?

Google recommends keeping business information complete and up to date, and says complete and accurate information can help a business appear in relevant local search results.

Hours deserve special attention.

If Google says you are open until 6 p.m. and a customer arrives at 5:15 to find the doors locked, that is more than a minor online error. You have created a disappointed customer.

Google also allows businesses to set special hours for holidays, events and other temporary changes rather than changing their regular schedule.

Put holiday-hour updates on the same checklist as changing the sign on the front door.

Your business category and service information matter, too.

Someone may know the name of your company and search specifically for it. But the larger marketing opportunity comes from people who do not know your name.

They search for things such as “electrician near me,” “best lunch nearby,” “oil change,” “roof repair” or “florist open now.”

Google says local search results are primarily influenced by relevance, distance and prominence. Providing complete and detailed information helps Google understand what a business does and match it with relevant searches.

So don't assume Google understands everything you sell simply because your business name is listed correctly.

Review your primary business category. Add appropriate services or products where available. Complete the attributes Google offers for your type of business.

item.title: Why Every Small Business Should Build an Email List — Even If Facebook Is Working
item.dc:creator: The Caledonian-Record Business Desk
item.description:
For many small businesses, social media feels like the easiest way to stay connected with customers. A Facebook post can reach hundreds or thousands of people in a few minutes. An Instagram account can show off new products, completed jobs or a busy Saturday morning. And if those channels are working, it can be tempting to think there is no reason to add another marketing task.

There is one problem: your followers are not really yours.

Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, Google and other platforms are extraordinarily useful, but they control the rules. An algorithm change can reduce your reach. An account can be suspended. A platform can lose popularity. Advertising costs can rise. None of those things mean a business should abandon social media. They do mean it is risky to make a third-party platform the only way you can reach people who already know and like your business.

An email list is an audience you can reach directly

An email list is different. Customers have given you permission to contact them, and you can reach that list without hoping an algorithm decides to show your post.

That makes email particularly useful for local businesses, where repeat customers and word of mouth often matter more than massive online reach. A hardware store does not need 100,000 followers. It may be far more valuable to have 1,000 local customers who have asked to hear about seasonal products, workshops or special offers. A restaurant can tell regular customers about a new menu. A contractor can share a spring maintenance checklist. A retailer can announce an event before posting it publicly.

The goal is not to email constantly. The goal is to have a reliable way to reach people when you actually have something worth telling them.

Start with a reason to sign up

“Join our email list” is not much of an invitation. Give customers a simple reason to say yes.

That reason does not always have to be a discount. A garden center might offer monthly planting tips. An auto shop could send seasonal maintenance reminders. A real estate office might offer a short local market update. A restaurant could give subscribers first notice of special dinners or holiday reservations.

The best offer is usually something closely connected to why customers already do business with you.

Make collection routine

You do not need a complicated campaign to start building a list. Put a signup form on your website. Add a link to your email signature and social profiles. Ask customers at checkout if they would like occasional updates. Include a signup link on invoices, receipts or appointment confirmations where appropriate.

What matters most is consistency. A business that adds five interested people a week will have more than 250 new contacts after a year. Those are people who have voluntarily raised their hands and said, in effect, “You may contact me again.”

Do not buy a list

A purchased database of thousands of email addresses may look more impressive than a homegrown list of a few hundred people, but the smaller list is usually much more valuable. People who never asked to hear from you are less likely to open your messages, more likely to mark them as spam and unlikely to become loyal customers.

Build the list gradually and get permission. Quality beats quantity.

You do not need a weekly newsletter

One reason small businesses avoid email marketing is the assumption that they are signing themselves up for another endless content obligation. They are not.

A useful monthly email is better than a weekly message nobody has time to write or read. Some businesses may only need to send when they have genuinely useful news.

A simple email can contain one helpful tip, one piece of business news and one clear next step. That is enough.

Use social media to grow what you own

This is not an argument against Facebook or any other platform. In fact, social media becomes more valuable when it helps build a direct customer relationship.

Use Facebook to attract attention. Use Google to help people find you. Use your website to explain what you do. Then give interested customers an easy way to stay connected directly.

The strongest small-business marketing systems do not depend entirely on any single channel. They use rented platforms to reach people while steadily building assets the business controls: its website, customer relationships, reputation and contact list.

If your Facebook page disappeared tomorrow, could you still reach your best customers?

If the answer is no, an email list is a good place to start.

This article is part of The Caledonian-Record’s Small Business Marketing series. The Caledonian-Record provides advertising and marketing services to local businesses, including some of the tools discussed in this article.
